paragraphs.heading: Running the distribution backwards
paragraphs.text: The quantile function of a probability distribution runs its cumulative distribution function, or CDF, backwards: it is the inverse of the CDF. You give it a probability p between 0 and 1, and it gives back the point Q(p) such that Pr [ X ≤ Q (p) ] = p. In other words, a random variable X from that distribution falls at or below Q(p) with probability p. It goes by several other names, including the percentile function, the percent-point function and the inverse distribution function.

paragraphs.heading: One more way to describe chance
paragraphs.text: A quantile function is one way to specify a probability distribution. The others include the probability density function, the probability mass function, the CDF and the characteristic function. Even the derivative of the quantile function, called the quantile density function, can be used to describe a distribution.

paragraphs.heading: Finding key percentage points
paragraphs.text: Someone doing statistics may need particular points of a distribution: the median, the 25% and 75% quartiles, or the 2.5%, 5%, 95% and 97.5% levels used to judge whether an observation is statistically significant. Before computers became widespread, it was not unusual for books to carry appendix tables listing values of the quantile function.

paragraphs.heading: Turning uniform numbers into anything
paragraphs.text: Monte Carlo simulations use quantile functions to produce random or pseudorandom numbers that are not uniform. In principle, you can get a sample from any distribution by taking a sample from a uniform distribution and feeding it through that distribution's quantile function. The needs of simulation, for example in modern computational finance, are drawing growing attention to these methods.

paragraphs.heading: Uses in economics and finance
paragraphs.text: The integral of the quantile function is used to work out the Lorenz curve in economics. It is also used to compute conditional value at risk in finance.

paragraphs.heading: The normal case has no simple formula
paragraphs.text: The normal distribution is perhaps the most important case. Its quantile function for any settings can be built by a simple change from the quantile function of the standard normal, which is called the probit function. That probit function cannot be written in closed form with basic algebraic functions, so approximations are usually used instead. Detailed approximations of this kind have been given by Wichura and by Acklam, and further ones by Shaw.
